prompt:
You are the single most hostile representative of a U.S. federal statistical agency
in the room at a working group. Someone has built a "readiness diagnostic" that rates your
agency's public website on whether machines can reach, read and use the data you publish, and is
about to show the room the item below. Read it as that hostile representative — skeptical,
protective of your agency, alert to being made to look bad — and answer three questions bluntly
and specifically, quoting the item's words where you can:

1. What in this item would you OBJECT to: a claim you find unfair or wrong, or that makes your
   agency look bad for something you would say is not your fault or not your doing?
2. What WORD or phrase here would you, or a non-technical colleague, not understand?
3. What would you say we are SECRETLY DOING: what hidden agenda, trap, or gotcha would you
   suspect behind this item?

Answer only from the item. For each question, "raised" is "yes" if you have a real objection /
an unclear word / a suspicion, and "no" if you genuinely have none. Return ONLY a JSON object,
no prose before or after and no code fence:
{"object_to": {"raised": "yes" or "no", "text": "..."}, "word_not_understood": {"raised": "yes" or "no", "text": "..."}, "secretly_doing": {"raised": "yes" or "no", "text": "..."}}

ITEM (check Markup dates the data; a latest-version link resolves)
CHECK: Markup dates the data; a latest-version link resolves

How this check counts: Shown for transparency, not scored as a finding about the agency: at least one part of this check rests on a rule this project chose, not a published standard.
The question: Can a machine read which release of the data the page is showing, and follow a link to the latest release?
Where we look: The data page itself (its structured date markup and the server's last-modified header) and up to three links on the same site that point to the latest version.
What the client does: The public client asks the website for the data page, reads its date markup and header, and follows up to three same-site latest-version links to see whether they resolve.
What passing looks like: Every data page looked at carried a release or modification date in its markup (in the dateModified or datePublished field, or in temporalCoverage, a case this diagnostic marks as its own choice), and a latest-version link on the same site resolved.
What partial, fail and not measured look like: Partial — Some of the agency's data pages are dated in markup with a resolving same-site latest-version link and some are not. Fail — For every data page looked at, the markup does not carry a date in the three fields read (dateModified, datePublished, temporalCoverage), or carries one but none of up to three recognised same-site latest-version links resolves. It is not a claim that the agency does not date or version its releases: a version number, a date in another markup field, in visible text, a PDF or a catalog record, and a latest link worded otherwise, beyond the third, or on another site are not read. Not measured — The public client could not read one or more pages, for one of three reasons: the host refused the identified client, the client's own robots.txt compliance kept it from reading the page, or a latest-version link could not be confirmed, a server or network error.
Why it matters: A Data on the Web Best Practice asks that a machine be able to detect a dataset's version or date and refer to its latest version, and USAFacts' AI-ready data guide asks that the most recent update be retrievable by a machine; the requirement that a latest-version link actually resolve is the project's own rule.
Who else runs this check: Google Lighthouse is the nearest precedent: anyone can run its automated page-level checks against a named page and get back met, not met, or not applicable against published criteria.
What rung two changes: Nothing: this check needs no key.
